notes: The external LED, resistor are optional; the tutorial's default uses the on-board LED on D13. The graph builds the optional external circuit.

Breadboard positions read from the circuit image: orange wire pin 13 -> column 3 row g; resistor column 3 to column 6 row h; LED anode (long, bent leg) in column 6 row i, cathode in column 8 row i; black wire from GND (next to pin 13, assumed GND.1) to column 8 row g.
The USB cable connects the Arduino to a computer for programming/power; its port is unspecified, and the computer is not a part.

The parts list says 3 hook-up wires, but the circuit image shows 5 jumper wires: red (5V to + rail), black (GND to - rail), teal (pin 2), orange (button to + rail) and a short black one (resistor to - rail). All 5 are included, and the image is treated as the authority.

Breadboard naming follows the catalogue: bank 't' is rows a-e and bank 'b' is rows f-j. In the image the half labelled f-j is drawn on top and a-e on the bottom. So the teal wire lands on 6b.j, and the button, resistor and the other wires sit in bank 't'.

The lower rail pair is used. The red-marked row is bp (+) and the black-marked row is bn (-). Rail hole numbers are counted from the left, with the first hole under the red and black wires as 1. The numbering is approximate.

The button straddles the centre gap. Only its two lower legs (columns 4 and 6, row e) are visible, so only one port per side is connected: 1.l at column 4 and 2.l at column 6. The other legs share the same strips on the other half of the board.

Side 1 of the button (column 4) goes to 5V through the orange wire. Side 2 (column 6) goes to pin 2 through the teal wire and to GND through the 10k pull-down resistor. The resistor runs from column 6 to column 9, and column 9 goes to the - rail.
The black wire from the Arduino enters the second GND pin in the POWER header, which is mapped to GND.2.
The resistor value prop is given as 10000 ohms, from the 10K ohm in the manual. The catalogue label says 100Ω, but the manual and schematic say 10kΩ.
The manual leaves GPIO pin choice and breadboard layout to the user; I used the pins from its full code listing: GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27 and GPIO10, which are physical pins 7, 11, 13 and 19.

Each button straddles the breadboard centre gap. Side 1 is in the top half and side 2 is in the bottom half. The GPIO lead goes into the top strip and a pin-to-pin jumper takes the bottom strip to the ground rail. The tutorial's wiring-a-button include is not shown, so this follows the standard layout.
The five pin-to-socket leads are four GPIO leads plus one ground lead from Pi pin 6 (GND) to rail tn.1. I assumed the socket end (a) goes on the Pi and the pin end (b) goes in the breadboard.
The four pin-to-pin jumpers connect each button's ground side to the tn rail. The rail is shared, so all grounds are common.
The buttons have no external pull-up or pull-down resistor because gpiozero Button uses the Pi's internal pull-up.
The catalogue rpi-4b has no 3.5mm audio jack port, so the speaker is joined to the Pi with no port named. The speaker's USB power connection is not shown in the manual and is not modelled.
The sample .wav files and the Python code are software and are not part of the graph.
